conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today.  
I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health specialist. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check how things have felt for you since your baby arrived. It’s simply a 10-question screening that helps us spot common mood and anxiety changes (and includes one question about self-harm) so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays confidential, and this is a judgment-free space; there are no “right” or “wrong” answers, just whatever has been true for you in the past seven days. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions together.

To start: overall, in the past week, how much have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not a whole lot. I’ll catch myself smiling every now and then—mostly when the baby does something cute—but I haven’t really laughed in days. It feels like the joy got dialed way down, and when something funny happens it just doesn’t hit the same as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’d say “not so much.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Um… not very often. I still look forward to a couple small things—like when my sister brings coffee—but mostly I wake up thinking “ugh, another day.” It’s like everything feels flat before it even starts.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong. I’ll replay small things—like not burping him long enough or missing a nap window—and convince myself it’s my fault. I know it sounds silly out loud, but in the moment it feels real.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. Even when everything’s quiet, my mind keeps spinning—what if he stops breathing, what if I’m not making enough milk, what if I miss something important. There’s rarely a real trigger; the worry just shows up and parks itself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits out of nowhere—my heart races, I feel shaky, and for a minute I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes, but those waves of panic catch me off guard a few times a week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… a lot of the time. It feels like the second I finish one thing, three more pile on—laundry, bottles, texts I forgot to answer, the baby’s next feeding. I’ll sit on the couch and just stare, frozen, because I can’t decide what to tackle first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week I laid there for hours—my body’s exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying everything I think I did wrong, worrying about tomorrow, and then I watch the clock tick past two, three in the morning.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… pretty much most days. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling that doesn’t really lift. I’ll cry when I’m feeding the baby, or while I’m folding onesies, and I can’t always explain why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

It happens… maybe twice this week. I’ll just be sitting there and suddenly the tears start. Nothing huge sets it off—just everything feeling too big and me feeling like I’m failing at all of it. When it starts, I can’t always stop right away, but it does taper off after a bit.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Yeah… it’s crossed my mind once or twice. Nothing planned—just those quick, scary flashes of “what if I weren’t here?” They pass in seconds, but they shake me up.

documents.highlight: A serial cross-sectional analysis of nearly 8 million (n 57,906,820) delivery hospitalizations identified in the National Inpa- tient Sample, representing almost 40 million (n539,024,974) deliveries in the United States occurring from 2006 to 2015, found that perinatal mood and anxietydisorders increased from 18.4 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 16.4 –20.0) to 40.4 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 39.3 – 41.6) and that severe mental illness increased from 4.2 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 3.9 –4.6) to 8.1 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 7.9 –8.4) (5).

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Period

Symptoms/Concerns
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re infant care  
- Marked anxiety (free-floating worry, panic episodes 3–4×/week)  
- Overwhelm, “frozen” spells, difficulty initiating tasks  
- Sleep-onset insomnia linked to rumination  
- Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting thoughts “what if I weren’t here”)

Patterns
- Symptoms present most days for ≥ past week, worse at night  
- Functional impact: difficulty completing infant care/household tasks, social withdrawal

Screening Significance
- Meets threshold indicators for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety  
- Safety risk: presence of any suicidal ideation warrants immediate further evaluation

Risk Factors Flagged
- Depressed mood, loss of pleasure, guilt, sleep disturbance, passive SI  
- No protective factors noted in responses

Next Step
- Refer for urgent clinical assessment (within 24 h) to rule out self-harm intent and determine level of care.
